title: Impact of NAFTA Tariff Removal on Bilateral Trade Flows

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
Difference-in-Differences (DID). NAFTA represents a policy shock that affected trade flows between member countries (treated group) at a specific time (post=1), while non-NAFTA country pairs serve as controls. The key assumption is parallel trends: absent NAFTA, trade flows between member and non-member country pairs would have followed similar trajectories. This assumption is plausible since global trade trends and macroeconomic conditions should affect all country pairs similarly.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load required libraries
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

# Read the data
data <- read_csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s44_data.csv")

# Main DID regression
did_model <- lm(y ~ treated + post + treat_x_post, data = data)

# Get robust standard errors
robust_se <- sqrt(diag(vcovHC(did_model, type = "HC1")))

# Print main results
cat("=== MAIN DID RESULTS ===\n")
cat("NAFTA Treatment Effect:", round(coef(did_model)["treat_x_post"], 4), "\n")
cat("Standard Error:", round(robust_se["treat_x_post"], 4), "\n")
cat("t-statistic:", round(coef(did_model)["treat_x_post"] / robust_se["treat_x_post"], 2), "\n")

# Summary of full model
summary(did_model)

# Robustness Check 1: Add unit fixed effects
fe_model <- lm(y ~ treated + post + treat_x_post + factor(unit_id), data = data)
cat("\n=== ROBUSTNESS: UNIT FIXED EFFECTS ===\n")
cat("Treatment Effect with Unit FE:", round(coef(fe_model)["treat_x_post"], 4), "\n")

# Robustness Check 2: Pre-trend test (if multiple pre-treatment periods exist)
pre_treatment <- data[data$post == 0, ]
if(length(unique(pre_treatment$period)) > 1) {
  # Test for differential pre-trends
  pre_trend_test <- lm(y ~ treated * factor(period), data = pre_treatment)
  cat("\n=== PRE-TREND TEST ===\n")
  print(summary(pre_trend_test))
}

# Robustness Check 3: Placebo test with random treatment assignment
set.seed(123)
data$placebo_treated <- sample(data$treated)
data$placebo_interact <- data$placebo_treated * data$post
placebo_model <- lm(y ~ placebo_treated + post + placebo_interact, data = data)
cat("\n=== PLACEBO TEST ===\n")
cat("Placebo Treatment Effect:", round(coef(placebo_model)["placebo_interact"], 4), "\n")

# Calculate percentage effect (since y is in logs)
percent_effect <- (exp(coef(did_model)["treat_x_post"]) - 1) * 100
cat("\n=== ECONOMIC INTERPRETATION ===\n")
cat("Percentage increase in bilateral trade:", round(percent_effect, 2), "%\n")
```

## 3. Expected Findings
I expect a positive and significant coefficient on the treatment interaction term (treat_x_post), likely between 0.2 to 0.8 in log terms, translating to roughly 20-120% increase in bilateral trade flows. This expectation is based on extensive empirical trade literature showing that tariff elimination substantially increases trade volumes through reduced trade costs. The magnitude should be economically significant given that NAFTA eliminated most tariffs between major trading partners (US, Canada, Mexico), creating substantial trade creation effects that outweigh potential trade diversion.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Comparing trade flows before and after NAFTA for treated and control pairs.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The tariff removal under NAFTA led to a significant increase in bilateral trade flows.
